en: In the *Āmaraughaśāsana*, the descent of the upward power (*ūrdhvaśaktinipāta*) is known through the fourfold bulb (*kandacatuṣṭaya*).

That water which originates from the moon, which resides in the supreme ether, and which is designated as the *liṅga*—that is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Below that, it supports the stable lotus, whose mouth is turned upward in the heart. (1.1)

Having performed the *kumbhaka* (retention) firmly established within oneself, that very same [breath] which has entered the *brahmanāḍī* is brought [upward]; this process, consisting of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvagā*), is called *sāraṇā*.
[1.2] The *ṣaḍadhvagā* is now described:

[2] From its base at the tip of the tongue, situated in the hollow of the temple-cavity like the clapper of a bell, it reaches the opening of the royal tooth (*rājadanta*) within the *śaṅkhinī*, with its face turned upward toward the edge. [2.1]

That lunar water which has entered the mouth by means of the method of the root of the jaw-cavity should all be protected within the abode of the Sun, who is the form of Time; this is the supreme extraction (*parā sāraṇā*).
[2.2] The supreme extraction is now described through another practice.

[3] If a man, dancing with his tongue perpetually upturned, drinks the flood of nectar from the stream of the mouth—which is delicious, cools the body, removes the fear of misfortune, and destroys hunger and thirst—[then he attains success]. [3.1]

"Indeed, from this, the stability of the *piṇḍa* arises; alas, the great diseases of death flee, misfortune goes to its destruction, and having wandered through time, it removes and brings an end to poison and old age.
[3.2] After *sāraṇā*, *sāraṇā* is described:

"Then, having led the tip of the tongue into the opening between the two front teeth (*rājadanta*), and having placed it upon the uvula (*ghaṇṭikā*), one should cast the digit (*kalā*) of the moon onto the joint of the uvula (*pratijihvā*) along the path. [4.1]

In this manner, streams of nectar fall into the *sāraṇī*, and then the six-faced *gāndhārī* also brings about the crushing of that cluster and the expansion of the opening of the channel (*nāḍīmukha*).
[4.2] Following *sāraṇā*, *pratisāraṇā* is described:
having led the lunar digit (*candrajā kalā*) upward by means of the vital breath (*prāṇavāta*) into the cavity (*koṭara*), [5.1]
[5.2] And by that practice of Gāndhāra, one churns [the breath] born of the divine.
Following Gāndhāra, Pratisāraṇā is described.

[6.1] When the vital breath (prāṇa) is made exceedingly long by the wind flowing through the posterior nasal passage, the virtuous perform the Pratisāraṇā with the lunar water (candrāmbu) along the path prior to the uvula (ghaṇṭikā).

Sprinkling [the seed], having come under the power of the vast fire of time (*kālaviśālavahni*), he brings those hundred channels back to life and makes them perform their function once more, like the trunk of a withered tree assuming a new body.
[6.2] Immediately after the process of rubbing (*pratisāraṇa*), the process of drawing up through the conch (*śaṅkhasāraṇā*) is described:
"The pair of testicles should be raised up, and the penis should be held erect between them; indeed, during the rite of *śaṅkhasāraṇā*, one's own mouth must be kept constantly turned upward. [7.1]
[7.2] Due to the binding of the body in all its positions, just as the water from a jar of nectar poured from the mouth of veins extracted from the *skandha* flows downward;
[8] by another method, the "conch-drawing" (*śaṅkhasāraṇā*) is described:
[8.1] "The drawing of the testicles should be performed, or else the 'conch-drawing'."
There should be the awakening of Kuṇḍalī and one should remain in the utkaṭāsana posture.
(8.2) Immediately after the śaṅkhasāraṇā, the mahāsāraṇā is described.

(9) Having taken up the collections of pure winds from the seat behind, the serpent-like power (bhujagī) should be established in the solar orb through the three channels that have arisen from the wound at the throat. (9.1)

The Goddess, arisen on the central path, produces trembling, and from that, fainting; then there is the vision of being drawn far away, and other great channels for the groups of auditory perceptions.
[9.2] The "Great Channel" (mahāsāraṇā) is described by way of its function:

the serpent-like channel arising from the bulbous root within the calyx of the foundational lotus, having joined with the triad of channels, reaches the pair of upper channels originating from the Moon and Sun, which have entered the path of non-duality. [10.1]

There, by pressing with the fingers in succession, the mind, the vital breath (*māruta*), and the moon attain peace; thereafter, the sun [is reached], and thus in this world, the "Great Consonance" (*mahāsāraṇā*) becomes equalized. (10.2) When the flood of the serpent [of the central channel] has reached the edge of the mouth of the moon’s consciousness within the sun, and the excessive contact with the wind has been withdrawn, she then swiftly runs forth.
(10.3) Producing tremors and other signs from the end of the glorious middle path, she—though filled with wrath—bestows the esteemed nectar upon the moon that travels along its very support. (10.4)

First, the drying [process] occurs here; thereafter, drawing-in (*sāraṇa*) must be performed, and great drawing-in (*mahāsāraṇa*) and counter-drawing-in (*pratisāraṇa*) should be carried out according to the sequence of the path indicated by the Guru.

(10.5) And only after that, in the procedure for the drawing-in of the conch (*śaṅkhasāraṇa*), great drawing-in should be performed; let the "fainting" (*sammūrchā*) in its expanded form be administered three times a day.

(10.6) Having contracted it into the form of an elephant's trunk, which has become immovable and bound within the body, one should breathe with the heart into the place known to be four finger-breadths below the top of the head, not too high. (10.7)

When the pair of winds is bound by the teeth through the embrace of close contact, the perfections of the mind arise on the path that is born from the simultaneous loosening and falling away of the knot at the navel. (10.8) When the wind has spread far outward and remains on the path from the navel, and when the three bindings are present yet relaxed, and the awakening of the center occurs; (10.9) then the two-seated wind is quickly held even as it is drawn upward in succession. Thus, through the drying up of the movement of the mind, one abides once the wind has reached its attainable state. (10.10)

At the root, in the upper wheel above the root, at the base of the family of the testicles, on the bank of the fire and the elephant, rich with trembling, agitation, and whirling, one attains the familiarity with sound; with hair standing on end from the descent of heat—[this is the state].

(10.11) The abandonment of the earth, poetic genius, entry into another's body, subjugation, and attraction—indeed, when consciousness has reached this state, it becomes capable of all these, as well as the established power of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*).
(10.12) Two Brahmans are to be known: the Brahman of Sound (*śabdabrahman*) and that which is the Supreme (*para*). (10.13)
In the heart, the supreme abode, are the sun and the moon in the center. Having grasped that resonance (nāda), one should unite consciousness (caitanya) with it.
Two Brahmans are to be known: the Brahman of Sound (śabdabrahma) and that which is the Supreme (para).
One who is proficient in the Word-Brahman attains the Supreme Brahman.
(10.17) Abandoning everything else, one should constantly practice the Word-Brahman.
(10.18) The Word-Brahman exists in two ways: that which is self-cognizable and that which is not cognizable. (10.19)
The first sound is "cinoti," the second is "ciñcinoti. The third would be "vivara," and the fourth is the sound of a conch shell. The fifth is the roar of a cloud, and this sixth is the utterance.

The seventh is called the sound of bronze cymbals, and the eighth is the sound of clouds. The ninth is the burning of fire, and the tenth is the resonance of a drum. This is the unstruck sound (anāhatanināda) emerging from the end of the wind.

But that which is without resonance (*dhvani*) and likewise lacks sound (*nāda*) is unwise. (10.26) Having extracted the essence, it gathers it; it gathers what rests within the *bhaga*. (10.27) It enters through the portion of the flavorless, accompanied by the sound of a cloud. (10.28)
The marrow falls with a sound as terrifying as the surging ocean;

the sound of the sky is like cymbals, and the resonance of the vital breath is like the thundering of clouds in succession. The individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed the burning fire, and liberation (*mokṣa*) becomes the state of equal flavor (*samarasa*).
In this way, one should perceive the pure self by means of the self within the self.

(10.32) In the first [case], there is affection for people; in the second, the destruction of disease. (10.33) By the third, there is poetic talent; and in the fourth, the power of attraction from afar. (10.34)
In the fifth, there is desire for speech; in the sixth, one should abandon the stage.
In the seventh, having gazed afar, in the eighth one becomes like a diamond.
In the ninth, the body throbs; in the tenth, there is the state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*).
In the midst of earth, earth exists, and likewise water in the midst of water;
(10.38) In the midst of fire, fire exists, and wind is dissolved into wind; (10.39) The entire collection of elemental bodies, together with their essential natures, dissolves into space. (10.40)
"Unstruck, Dhanañjaya resounds day and night.
When the yogi mounted there attains the supreme state.

[10.41–42] This is the differentiation of the primary constituents (*prakṛti*): earth, water, fire, air, and ether; these five qualities are the great elements (*mahābhūta*) within the body, and therein they exist in fivefold ways. [11]
Bone, flesh, skin, channels, and hair—these are the five qualities of earth.
Saliva, urine, tears, nasal mucus, and sweat—these are the five qualities of water.
Hunger, thirst, sleep, laziness, and lustre—these are the five qualities of fire.
Vāyu possesses five qualities: flowing, leaping, contracting, expanding, and obstructing.

Ākāśa possesses five qualities: passion, hatred, shame, fear, and delusion. Thus, the five elements are adorned with these five qualities each. Sound, touch, taste, form, and smell are the five qualities of the gross elements.
The nine dramatic sentiments (rasas) beginning with the erotic (śṛṅgāra) are the [resultant] states (bhāvas) of the comic (hāsya) and so forth. 18.
And there are six tastes (āsvādas): pungent, bitter, astringent, sour, sweet, and salty. 19.
And there are two types of karma: auspicious and inauspicious. 20.
The ten vital winds (vātas) are: prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, vyāna, nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya.
(21) The seventy-two thousand channels (nāḍīs), beginning with iḍā, piṅgalā, suṣumnā, gāndhārī, hastijihvā, yaśasvinī, pūṣā, lambusā, kuhū, and śaṅkhinī, [are located there].
(22) And the three paths are: origination, maintenance, and dissolution. (23)
There is a heap of bones numbering three hundred and sixty; with this [body] there is a connection through the vital breath.

(24) Desire, anger, greed, delusion, intoxication, pride, and egoism—these are the seven bonds. (25) Discrimination, awakening, contentment, joy, horripilation, forbearance, tranquility, meditation, knowledge, festivity, passion, dispassion, bliss, trembling, fainting, transformation, mental impressions (*vāsanā*), and so forth, are the essential natures of *prakṛti*. (26)
There are three and a half crores of body hairs.
(27) Wind, bile, and phlegm constitute the three fundamental humors (*prakṛti*).
(28) Wind is the fundamental nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*); bile arises from fire; and phlegm comes into being through obstruction. (29)
Skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen, *prāṇa*, *jīva*, and *śakti*—these are the ten constituents (*dhātu*).
(30) The two apertures of breath, the two apertures of the eyes, the two apertures of the ears, the two apertures of the mouth, and the two apertures of excretion—these are the ten gates.
(31) Now, the tenth gate is twofold: the path of semen, which is the nectar (*amṛta*), and the path of time (*kāla*), located at the base of Brahmā’s staff between the sun and the moon.

There is a vulva-shaped [region]; therefore, there exists a western *liṅga* supported by the Brahma-staff (*brahmadaṇḍa*) that has come from there. By the word "western" (*paścima*), a location is indicated;
in its center, there is a *liṅga*-shaped form.

(32) For men, it is the path of semen (*retas*); for women, it is the path of menstrual blood (*rajas*). Together with that, at the time of the flower (*puṣpasamaya*) supported by the line of the Brahma-staff, the female's *rajas* flows, having arrived through the entire collection of all-pervading channels (*nāḍī*). (33)

In that very state, from the union of the poison-remover and the stainless one through the casting of the seed, there is the arrival of bliss; he who is the agent of both the time of dissolution and the time of poison is the Stainless One (Nirañjana).
(34) When the mind is pierced by the three powers, from the seed and the stainless one, he who produces the bliss of the steps of Vajra-worship is Manmatha. (35–36)
When the mind is satisfied, there is liberation of the mind once the fire has ascended the upper path.
They know the semen moved by the *udāna* wind to be the poison of the line of death.
That which exists within the center of the mind, resting upon a space as subtle as a hundredth part of the tip of a hair—[that is the state]. (37–39)
That which is free from all states of existence is declared to be the stainless (nirañjana).
The power (śakti) rests upon the stainless, and by that subtle power, it is supported;
it takes refuge in the mind—this is to be known as the triad of powers.

The seed arises from the three powers; from the seed comes desire (*kāma*), and from that, poison (*viṣa*). Desire is said to be of the nature of creation (*sṛṣṭi*), while poison becomes the state of death.

What need is there for much? For those who are stainless (*nirañjana*) through the removal of the poison of desire, there is residence in the sprout at the root of Brahma’s staff. Through these [means], liberation is face-to-face; for one whose body has been reduced to ashes, there is no further returning to rebirth.
"Alas, the foolishness of the world! Some say that liberation is the cessation of good and evil karma;
some say that liberation is based on the recitation of the Vedas;
and some say that liberation is characterized by the absence of any support."

Some say that liberation is characterized by form (*rūpa*), the drop (*bindu*), sound (*nāda*), the mass of consciousness (*caitanyapiṇḍa*), and space (*ākāśa*), through the possibility of practice connected with the performance of the art of meditation.
(49) Some say that liberation is characterized by bliss (*ānanda*) arising from the attachment to worship, the worshiper, wine, meat, and sexual union.
(50) Some say: (51)
Liberation is characterized by the movement of Kuṇḍalinī, which is awakened from the root-center (mūlādhāra).
(52) Some say that liberation is characterized by the falling of the gaze of *susumā*; however, liberation does not consist in characteristics based on such types of mental cultivation.
(53) Now, the state of liberation is described: where, through the process of innate absorption (*sahajasamādhi*), the mind beholds the mind—that indeed is liberation. (54)
The abode that destroys the poison of desire arises from the mind; within the mind, as the primary cause, the processes of origination, maintenance, and dissolution proceed.
And it was said by the Blessed Maheśvara:
"O Goddess, in the state of liberation while living, the mind is a seed free from taint."
"The yogi situated on the path of death, having understood this, should practice his action.
(58) Thus, by this path, the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) becomes stable.

(59) Now follows the explanation of the arrangement of the piercing of the *śaṅkhinī* channel as it arises from the action of *dhāraṇā*: between the anus and the penis is the circle of the vulva (*bhaga-maṇḍala*), which is triangular and has three whorls.

It is said that there are one, two, or three knots (*granthi*) therein. Among these one, two, or three knots, at a distance from the knots, there stands a four-petaled lotus facing downwards. In the center of its pericarp (*karṇikā*), there is a conch-spiral (*śaṅkhāvarta*) the size of a lotus fiber (*mṛṇālasūtra*).

Therein resides the Kuṇḍalinī power, resembling a sprout of coral, consisting of two or three channels (*nāḍī*), which has entered the mouth of the seed of consciousness (*caitanya-bīja*) and is asleep. 60.
There, in the middle of the three paths, she remains in a subtle state;
having a form resembling a thread of wool, she has entered the circle of the navel,
measuring four finger-breadths and coiled eightfold in shape.
It vibrates within the center of the navel, branching out in many ways.
The wheel (cakra) resting upon ten channels is proclaimed to be in the center of the navel;
these are Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā as the third.
For these stand on the upward path, suspended from great branches;
Jayantī and Alambuṣā alone hang from a great branch.
That Praṇītā is indeed established by many in Brahmāvarta.

By means of the Brahma-staff wheel (*brahmadaṇḍacakra*), [the nectar flows] as far as the skull-bowl (*kapālakarpara*). Within that skull-bowl, the Skull-Linga situated inside the lunar disc (*candramaṇḍala*) above the location of Lampikā pours down a stream of nectar (*amṛtadhārā*).
That very nectar, having been restrained by the Śaṅkhinī at the base of the Brahma-staff within the cavity of the royal tooth (*rājadanta*), flows forth into the center of the head.
The single opening of the mouth, situated between the two upper front teeth, is called the "mouth of Śaṅkhinī" and the "tenth door.

At that place, at the end of the circle of the root-genitals, the Kuṇḍalinī power has emerged; there, the Soma-nāḍī arises from the left side and the Sūrya-nāḍī arises from the right side. The Moon pervades the left limb, and the Sun pervades the right limb. The Moon... [is] the Moon.
The left nostril is in the left limb and the right nostril is in the right limb; thus are the Sun and Moon situated.

(71) Wherein, in the root-knot (*mūlakanda*), there is the arising of the wind, the arising of the mind, the arising of the sun, the arising of the individual soul (*jīva*), the arising of sound, and the arising of the letters of the Mātṛkā.
(72) In the center of the mind, the stainless Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the object of sleep, desire, and action. (73)
The wind, arising from the path of the moon and sun, exerts itself at the root-knot (mūlakanda);
situated within the support of the power (śakti), it moves along, piercing the staff of Brahmā (brahmadaṇḍaka).
As for that power which resides in the root-knot, its form is coiled like a serpent (kuṇḍalākāra). // 74–76 //

This wind of the upward-rotating vortex is called *prāṇa* by the wise. (77) When the female serpent is whirled upward by the stalk of the *kanda* and its powerful coils, she becomes faint; thus established, she perceives Śiva through the vital breaths alone. (78–79)

From the position of birth downwards, that sign (*liṅga*) is situated in the middle of the class of the foundational bulb (*ādhārakanda*); it is secret, and above that is the station of the sign, the *svādhiṣṭhāna*. In the region of the navel, in the upper portion of the *maṇipūraka*, is the fire-element (*analaka*); by means of that, [the breath] reaches the *uddaṇḍaka* and so forth. In the lower region of the *maṇipūraka*, situated to the south-west, is the place of impurity (*amedhya*) in the center.

From the navel arises the *kanda*, shaped like a lotus; there, it is said, is the support for the channels of the body. In the heart is the earth element (*pṛthivītattva*), yellow in color and in the center shaped like a *kadamba* bud; that is the place where the mind finds rest, and it is the fire-wheel (*analacakra*). In the throat is the self-element (*ātmatattva*), filled with the flow of water; that is the place of purification (*viśuddhisthāna*). In the middle of the palate, it has the form of a lamp flame.

The ever-shining light is the *tejas-tattva* (the fire principle); the *vāyu-tattva* (the air principle) is in the sprout of the cavity of the skull; the *ākāśa-tattva* (the space principle) is at the tip of the nose. Above that is the station of the *ājñā* (the command). Within the station of the *ājñā*, amidst the sixteen knots, is the sixteenth digit (*kalā*) of nectar. Within that, resting like a hundredth part of the tip of a hair, is at its end, above that, at the conclusion of the digits, the *bindu*. Immediately following the piercing of the *bindu*, there is the region of the head shaped like a *śṛṅgāṭaka* (a triangle).

In that [state] is the station of the dissolution of the mind; endowed with the non-duality of the mind’s bondage to the body, it is the abode of the three worlds. Residing therein is the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*). Thus, adorned by these three powers, he is the reflection in the mirror of consciousness (*ciddarpaṇa*), equal [to all], yet characterized by the various portions of phenomenal existence (*bhāva-kalā*).
Skilled in observing the activities of *saṃsāra*, he who appears in the state of deep sleep as a formal being like the moon in water—that is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
The Great Lord (Maheśvara) is all-pervading and the creator of the fourteenfold collection of living beings; such is this Supreme Self (Paramātman). 80.
